topic: Machine Learning: Classification vs Regression Scenarios

questions.scenario: A fintech corporation is designing an automated credit risk engine. The raw dataset contains severe zero-inflation: 97% of transactions result in zero financial loss, while 3% incur continuous, highly variable dollar losses ranging from $500 to $100,000. The initial engineering approach used a single Gradient Boosted Regressor optimizing Mean Squared Error (MSE) to predict exact financial loss amounts directly. In production, the model consistently predicts near-zero loss values for all users, completely missing high-risk default cases.
questions.question: Which architectural re-framing mathematically addresses this zero-inflated continuous distribution while maintaining high sensitivity to financial loss risk?
options: A) Formulate a two-stage (Hurdle/Two-Part) architecture using a binary classification model to predict default probability, coupled with a conditional regression model trained solely on non-zero loss instances.
B) Replace the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function in the single regressor with Mean Absolute Error (MAE) to reduce sensitivity to zero-value clusters.
C) Apply a log transformation to the target variable and retain the single continuous regression framework using Ordinary Least Squares.
D) Convert the target continuous loss into 100 equal-width discrete bins and train a standard multi-class classification model.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Formulate a two-stage (Hurdle/Two-Part) architecture using a binary classification model to predict default probability, coupled with a conditional regression model trained solely on non-zero loss instances.
questions.explanation: Zero-inflated targets with continuous positive values present a non-Gaussian, point-mass mixture distribution. Single regression models optimizing MSE minimize global loss by pulling predictions toward the dominant zero-mass mean. A two-stage Hurdle model resolves this by decomposing $P(Loss, Default) = P(Default) \times E[Loss | Default > 0]$. Stage 1 handles discrete class risk via classification (handling imbalance using cross-entropy or focal loss), and Stage 2 models the continuous severity conditional on a non-zero event.

questions.scenario: An e-commerce platform requires dynamic price optimization during user checkouts within a strict sub-50ms SLA limit. The input feature space contains over 100,000 sparse categorical features (search queries, sparse user tag vectors, and item interaction histories). An initial Deep Neural Network Regressor predicting continuous Willingness-To-Pay (WTP) achieved accurate offline RMSE but breached the inference SLA, averaging 250ms per request due to complex non-linear matrix multiplications.
questions.question: Which system design strategy provides the best trade-off between inference speed and feature density without losing dynamic pricing capability?
options: A) Switch to a Support Vector Regression (SVR) model utilizing a high-dimensional Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel.
B) Discretize the continuous price spectrum into fine-grained ordinal price tiers and deploy a regularized sparse Linear/Logistic Classifier using dot-product scoring.
C) Use t-SNE to reduce the 100,000 sparse features down to 10 dense components, then pass them to a 500-tree Random Forest Regressor.
D) Apply One-Hot Encoding to all sparse features and train an unpruned Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (GBDT) regressor.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Discretize the continuous price spectrum into fine-grained ordinal price tiers and deploy a regularized sparse Linear/Logistic Classifier using dot-product scoring.
questions.explanation: In ultra-low latency environments (sub-50ms SLA) with high-dimensional sparse inputs ($100k+$ dimensions), non-linear deep models, tree ensembles, and kernel methods (SVR RBF) incur prohibitive $O(N_{trees} \times depth)$ or $O(N_{support\_vectors} \times d)$ compute costs. Discretizing continuous WTP into ordinal tiers converts regression into a linear sparse classification problem. Sparse linear/logistic scoring requires only simple vector inner products ($O(k)$ where $k \ll d$ active non-zero features), easily executing under 5ms while maintaining price granularity.

questions.scenario: A hospital's intensive care unit (ICU) deploys an AI system to monitor continuous vital signs for predicting patient sepsis onset within 6 hours. Clinicians demand actionable binary alerts ('Intervene' vs 'Monitor') subject to a strict operational constraint: the False Alarm Rate (False Positive Rate) must strictly remain below 2% to avoid alarm fatigue. The vendor delivered a Ridge Regression model predicting a continuous 'Sepsis Severity Index' from 0.0 to 100.0.
questions.question: Why is framing this problem as continuous regression fundamentally inferior to a calibrated probabilistic classification model for setting threshold-based clinical alerts?
options: A) Ridge Regression optimization forces all continuous predictions to be strictly between 0 and 1, preventing custom thresholding.

B) Regression models optimize residual sum of squares (distance error) rather than likelihood, producing unbounded output scores that do not represent posterior probabilities $P(Sepsis|Vitals)$ required for precise Neyman-Pearson risk control.
C) Probabilistic classification automatically removes the need for feature normalization, whereas Ridge Regression degrades when handling real-time vital streams.
D) Continuous regression models cannot generate Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) or Precision-Recall curves.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Regression models optimize residual sum of squares (distance error) rather than likelihood, producing unbounded output scores that do not represent posterior probabilities $P(Sepsis|Vitals)$ required for precise Neyman-Pearson risk control.
questions.explanation: Regression models optimize distance-based metrics (e.g., $L_2$ distance / MSE), generating unbounded predictions that lack probabilistic interpretation. Setting arbitrary post-hoc threshold cutoffs on regression scores does not map to true underlying event probabilities $P(Y=1|X)$. A probabilistic classifier (e.g., Logistic Regression or Calibrated XGBoost) trained via Log-Loss / Cross-Entropy directly estimates posterior class probabilities. This enables decision-theoretic threshold tuning (Neyman-Pearson framework) to strictly bound the False Positive Rate at $\le 2\%$ based on explicit risk-cost matrices.
